questions.question_text: Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = e^{3x^{2}}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Differentiated the index as well as bringing it down; the index stays $3x^{2}$.
Left out the inner derivative $6x$ required by the chain rule.
Multiplied by the index itself instead of by the derivative of the index.

questions.question_text: Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = e^{1-4x^{3}}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Lost the negative sign when differentiating $1 - 4x^{3}$.
Replaced the index with its own derivative; the index must stay $1 - 4x^{3}$.
Reduced the power of $x$ without multiplying by the index $3$, giving $-4x^{2}$ instead of $-12x^{2}$.

questions.question_text: Use the product rule to differentiate $y = xe^{5x}$. Give your answer in factored form.

options.why: Multiplied the two derivatives together instead of using $u'v + uv'$.
Used $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{5x}\right) = e^{5x}$, omitting the factor $5$.
Kept only the $uv'$ term and dropped $u'v$.

questions.solution_text:
$y = xe^{5x}$
Product rule with $u = x$ and $v = e^{5x}$:
$y' = u'v + uv'$
$= 1\left(e^{5x}\right) + x\left(5e^{5x}\right)$
$= e^{5x}(1 + 5x)$

questions.question_text: Use the quotient rule to differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^{4x}}{x+2}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Added instead of subtracted when combining $4x + 8 - 1$ in the numerator.
Used $\dfrac{uv' - u'v}{v^{2}}$, reversing the order of the two numerator terms.
Differentiated the numerator and the denominator separately instead of using the quotient rule.

questions.question_text: Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = \left(e^{4x}-1\right)^{2}$. Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Left out the inner derivative $4e^{4x}$ of the bracket.
Used $e^{4x}$ as the inner derivative instead of $4e^{4x}$.
Expanded $\left(e^{4x}-1\right)^{2}$ as $e^{8x}-1$, dropping the middle term.

questions.question_text: To differentiate $y = e^{x^{2}+7x}$ by the chain rule, which choice of inner function $u$ and $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ is correct?

options.why: Copied the index instead of differentiating it.
Chose the base as the inner function; the inner function is the index.
Named the derivative of the index as the inner function, differentiating one step too far.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = e^{x^{2}-3x}$, find the exact value of $f'(3)$.

options.why: Evaluated $f(3) = e^{0} = 1$ instead of the derivative.
Used $2x = 6$ as the inner derivative, forgetting the $-3$ from $x^{2}-3x$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = xe^{4x}$ has exactly one stationary point. Find its $x$-coordinate.

options.why: Solved $4x - 1 = 0$, dropping the sign when solving $1 + 4x = 0$.
Set $e^{4x} = 0$, but an exponential is never zero.
Solved $x + 4 = 0$, reading the factor as $x+4$ rather than $1+4x$.

questions.solution_text:
$y = xe^{4x}$
Product rule with $u = x$ and $v = e^{4x}$:
$y' = 1\left(e^{4x}\right) + x\left(4e^{4x}\right)$
$= e^{4x}(1 + 4x)$
Stationary when $y' = 0$, and $e^{4x}$ is never zero.
$1 + 4x = 0$
$x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$
